title: The Cameronians: no harm to the intellect's freedom
source_text: LX. Neque tamen quicquam hic officit libertati, sive ex parte intellectus, sive ex parte voluntatis. Non ex parte intellectus, quia erga ipsum gratia haec duo tantum praestat, primo ut Evangelica veritas in convenienti luce ipsi proponatur: Deinde ut in statum congruentem restituatur, aut etiam aliquantum supra naturae sortem evehatur. Licet autem intellectus non possit vero agnito assensum non praebere, nulla tamen vis ipsi a proposita veritate affertur, dum assentitur vero, & in eo naturae suae maxime congruenter agit: ac proinde si qua species libertatis ipsi competit, hac in parte nihil laeditur. Et multo minus interna gratiae operatio, quae aut amissas vires intellectui restituit, aut etiam novas sufficit, praejudicare potest libertati intellectus, si quam habere censetur.
pass_a_gloss: LX. Nor yet does anything here hinder freedom, whether on the part of the intellect, or on the part of the will. Not on the part of the intellect, because toward it grace performs only these two things, first that the Evangelical truth be set before it in a fitting light: Next that it be restored to a fitting state, or even be raised somewhat above the lot of nature. And although the intellect cannot refuse assent to the truth known, yet no force is brought on it by the truth set forth, while it assents to the truth, & in that acts most agreeably to its nature: and therefore if any kind of freedom belongs to it, in this respect it is in no way hurt. And much less can the internal operation of grace, which either restores lost powers to the intellect, or even supplies new ones, prejudice the freedom of the intellect, if it is thought to have any.
pass_b_english: Thesis LX. Nothing here harms freedom, they say, either in the intellect or in the will. Not in the intellect, since grace does only two things for it: it sets the Gospel truth before it in a fitting light, and it restores it to a fitting condition, or even lifts it somewhat above its natural lot.

The intellect cannot withhold assent from a truth it has recognized, but the truth put before it does it no violence when it assents, since in assenting it acts entirely in keeping with its nature. So if the intellect has any sort of freedom, that freedom suffers no harm here.
Still less can the inward working of grace, which gives back to the intellect the powers it had lost or even supplies new ones, damage whatever freedom the intellect is thought to have.
